utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. And good morning to you, Madam Registrar. If you could be kind enough to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are here. From amongst the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Meek, Ms. Nikolic and Mr. Haynes. Prosecution is represented by lead counsel, Mr. McCloskey, and also Mr. Thayer. I understand that you have some preliminaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. Krgovic, my LiveNote is not working. I think what happened is certain people -- perhaps it could be attended to whilst Mr. McCloskey is addressing the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have the same problem. And my technical colleague is trying to sort it out but we still have the problem actually, but in the meantime we are trying to follow on the other --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. There is no problem at the moment, Your Honour, just while the preliminaries are going on I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- technical matters could proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for your cooperation. In the meantime, Madam Registrar, I think she is attending to the matter. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These words really shouldn't be too necessary, especially if I make any promises, we don't want them in the record. I just wanted to give the Court and counsel a little background where we are with witnesses. The good news is we have about 16 witnesses left for the case, with an additional seven as part of the motion to add witnesses. We appear to be on schedule to finish up those witnesses in November or December. That of course depends on, well, cross-examinations and directs but some cross-examinations, as you know, have been very quick. Other times they go very long but it looks like we are on schedule for that. And most of those witnesses, we have blocked out for particular weeks and some particular days because there is some international witnesses that -- such as General Smith, that are almost impossible to get unless you give them particular days. And so that's looking good. What is not looking so good is the present. We have three witnesses for this week. As you know, we lost Mr. Petrovic because he has been unwilling to come. (redacted) is not unwilling but he had a lawyer change just the last couple of days and it's not any fault of his and that the lawyer that he wants and the lawyer that we know and that will do a good job of representing him is not available for another few weeks. So that takes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Both those were significant witnesses and even with our one day of blackout that has put us in a situation where makeup is very difficult. We had a third witness, Mr. Fortin, [phoen] and there has been issues related to him that is going to cause a delay that he had some issues and then we have some things that we need to sort out before he can be called so that was -- we thought we were going to have him this week but it just is not going to work out that way. So those are -- with those three witnesses off creating this gap, we have been unable to pull anyone else in. We had a chance at getting Mr. Vasic but that posed some issues with some of the Defence counsel that in terms of preparation and it wasn't clear we could get him anyway, so we decided because the Defence counsel request not to try to put him in there either. So I see that we have very long estimates for cross-examination, which, if they hold out, would mean that we could go three or four days this week but I doubt very much these cross-examination estimates will be that long. And if we could go into private session for just one second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to have the part of your statement which was in private session made public?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President, I think it is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But I don't need to say it over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. I'm being practical and asking to you be too. So let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. What I was referring to here is page 933 of the transcript, lines 2 to 8 for the first issue and lines 9 to 18 for the second issue. And on both of these occasions, the witness stated very clearly that he did not say what was included in the proofing notes prepared by the Prosecution and which were given to us before his testimony began. Accordingly, Mr. President, in these circumstances, it is important, we believe, to know what the Prosecution's position is concerning these proofing notes. In other words, did the witness change his story during his testimony or did the Prosecution provide us with incorrect information in the proofing notes? In the light of the Prosecution's position that PW-108 would not have any reason to lie about Drago Nikolic, we think, Mr. President, that this is a very important question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we stand by our proofing notes, as we stand by our witness statements. I think that goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I have invited counsel before to argue or give our position, various positions on various witnesses, after they testify, to help keep the Court up-to-date on the positions. I'm still willing to do that. Before I would go into anything in depth on this witness, we of course would need to discuss that and Mr. Thayer would be the person that would be in the best position to argue that. I can tell you that that question about Drago Nikolic was clearly based on our view that this witness had -- that nothing in the cross-examination gave us any indication of why he would lie on Drago Nikolic personally. He hardly knew the man. That was what that question was designed to. We heard lots of questions about a potential conspiracy and involvement in 1992 which frankly I didn't -- don't think we have enough evidence to make a judgement on his involvement in 1992. Was he involved more than he says he was? Probably. Do I have facts to -- where I can argue that? No, I don't. But if you would like us to discuss that witness more -- in more detail and our viewpoint of that witness, we can and we are willing to, as we are with other witnesses because with some 150 witnesses, it sometimes -- you may not understand or remember where we are coming from on these witnesses, and so I have no objection to that, but I think of course we stand by our proofing notes and Mr. Bourgon should and will argue that proofing note which is in evidence and ask you to take inferences and of course that's his right and his duty and we expect him and hope that he does that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, very quickly, the issue is, and as I mentioned at the beginning when I stood up this morning, under normal circumstances, this would not be a question that we would even ask. What we get from the Prosecution, it is our understanding that this is correct information and that there is no question about that. We would not even think that the Prosecution could provide us with incorrect information unless it was a mistake but it did -- in this issue, because they themselves raised the issue that this man is telling the truth about Drago Nikolic, and there is a clear contradiction between the proofing notes and what he's saying, that's why we raised the issue this morning. Now, those two issues, Mr. President, were quite clear. This witness says prior to 1995, his friend said something that Drago Nikolic was involved in intelligence and security. That's what the proofing note says. The witness says no, I never said that, and then the witness went on to say in those proofing notes the meeting may have been in the commander or deputy commander's office and then the witness says no, no, no, it's for sure the meeting never took place in that office. So there is two clear contradictions and then we take the understanding that the proofing notes would be the correct version. But because they asked the question and they say you've got no reason to lie, then we are a bit puzzled and that's why we raise this issue this morning. I don't think we need to go any further into it, thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think either, unless my colleagues have a different view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We agree that we should leave it at that. Later on, of course, it becomes incumbent on us to evaluate this witness like every other witness and like every other piece of evidence that we have. Incidentally, for a while this morning, Judge Stole will not be with us. He had an appointment which couldn't be moved to any other time or any other day, although he tried. As soon as he finishes with that appointment, he will be joining us. Those of you who have been living in The Hague for long years know how difficult it is to shift appointments of certain nature in particular. All right. Just -- I just want to make sure that the next witness that we have -- first of all, have we exhausted the preliminary issues, preliminary matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This witness should have a caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But he has no protective measures in place, does he?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, he did not ask for any and so he does not have any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Trkulja, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You're about to start giving evidence and before you do so, our rules require that you enter or make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Usher is handing you the text. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. So you are soon going to start giving evidence. Mr. McCloskey will go first, and he will then be followed by the various Defence teams who will put questions to you on cross-examination. Your responsibility is to answer each and every question truthfully and to the best of your ability and try to -- please try to be as concise as possible. However, because you are a person who lived those times and were involved in some of the events happening during those days in your public function at the time, official function at the time, I am bound by one of our rules to alert you to a right that you have. There may be some questions put to you by either the Prosecution or the Defence which, if answered truthfully by you could possibly expose you to some criminal proceedings. I'm not saying that there will be such questions but there could be such questions, so I don't know because I don't know what questions the various lawyers here will be putting to you. If we come to that stage where you consider that answering a particular question could possibly expose you to criminal proceedings, then you have a right to draw our attention and ask us to exempt you from giving an answer to such questions. This is not, however, to be interpreted by you as an absolute right, in the sense that we have two options. We can agree with you and exempt you from answering such questions or we can disagree with you and compel you to answer such questions. If we compel you to answer such questions, then you have a further right. Provided your answers have been truthful, in other words, that they do not amount to false testimony, then whatever you may state in answering such questions cannot be used against you in any future criminal proceedings. And that's the ultimate right that you enjoy. Have you understood my explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you for that. And with that, I think I can pass him on to you, over to you, Mr. McCloskey. Thank you. You still estimate three hours for direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Probably not. Maybe half that, though it's hard to say. We have some documents we may go over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you first state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Good morning. Nedeljko Trkulja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are you a retired army officer?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what army did you retire from?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: The army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what year did you retire?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And at what rank did you -- were you when you retired?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, well, now, let's go back and can you tell us how old you are now?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: 66 -- 65, going on 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I grew up in Kikinda in the north of Banat which is in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Grkovci, Grahovo municipality, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you briefly outline your education and your military training and education?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I completed the entire military training, the officers school, the military academy and the command and staff military school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you graduated from the military academy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where -- what academy was that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: That was the academy of the army of Yugoslavia, the military academy of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And when did you graduate from the command and staff college?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you briefly outline your various positions, what kind of unit you were in and what kind of jobs you held, just as up to 1992? Just take a couple of minutes to give us a basic background.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. A platoon commander in the Skopje armoured brigade. I was there for four years. A company commander in the same unit for two years. The deputy commander of the battalion for two years in the same unit. For three years I was the battalion commander in Prilep. Again, that's when I finished the command and staff college. Then for three years, I was the desk officer for training in Kumanovo and then for four years I was in a motorised brigade. For four years I was the Chief of Staff of the same brigade. The chief of the armoured units of the Kumanovo corps and in the meantime, I don't know when exactly, I can't remember, I was a brigade commander and the corps that I served with was known as the Leskovac corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. At one point you say you were the chief of the armoured units of the Kumanovo corps. Are you an armour officer basically by training and background?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when were you the chief of the armoured units of that corps?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: From 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And when did you become a member of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I received the order in 1993. It came from the Leskovac corps. It was handed to me by General Bozidar Djokic. That was on the 9th of December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what were your orders?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: To be transferred to the 30th staff centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The 30th personnel centre?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, you can call it a personnel centre and it was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: To Han Pijesak, and I was assigned to be the chief of the armoured units of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. As -- when did you actually begin your tenure as chief of the armoured units for the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: On the 10th of December 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you chief of the armoured units in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, and let's talk a little bit about the structure as it was in July 1995. As the chief of the armoured units, who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: My superior was General Manojlo Milovanovic, the chief of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So were the armour -- chief of the armoured units was part of the staff that was led by the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's stay in 1995. Generally, was General Milovanovic -- where was he during a large part of 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: He was mostly at the Main Staff. However, at the relevant moment, the moment that you are interested in, I believe, although I can't be sure, because it was a long time ago, I believe that at that time he was in the western part of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Was he having to deal with the Croat advances in the Krajina area?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I believe so, but I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And now, when he wasn't at the offices, this shelter at Crni Rijeka and he was far away, like in the Krajina, did anyone replace him in the basic daily tasks of the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: For the most part, when we are talking about daily tasks, he would also be replaced by the chief of the administration, of the operations administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in July of 1995, who was that that would -- that replaced General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: That was General Radovan [as interpreted] Miletic, the chief of the operations administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've had a chance to look at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. McCloskey. I just want to confirm with the witness because of what we have in the transcript here, 17, line 1. What was the first name of General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Radivoje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's because in the transcript, it's Radovan so--

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've had a chance before testifying today to look at some of the reports of the -- from the Main Staff to the Presidency; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think I provided you from about 1st of July through 17 July, something like that? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I believe that you showed them up to the 20th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Up to the 20th. And under whose name were all those reports typed in?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I drafted them, and Miletic signed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll go over a couple of those reports to show that, but you noticed -- well, we spoke briefly about the fact that in the -- General Miletic is signed off on these reports as standing in for the Chief of Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes. He wasn't actually standing in for him, but that's how those reports were signed, and this was as much his mistake as mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "his mistake," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I mean General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you explain to us what the mistake was?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: The mistake was on my part to tell the typist to put, "standing in for" instead of "replacing" and the mistake on his part was that he did not delete this mistake of mine and replace it by the word "replacing."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us your understanding of the difference between the military status of replacing and standing in?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: If somebody is replacing somebody else, it can be for an hour, for two hours. He doesn't become a member of the inner command. He cannot issue orders to the assistants of the commander. The only thing that that person can do is to receive mail and dispatch mail to the chiefs of various army branches. As an operative, he cannot do that. Whereas when somebody stands in for somebody else, we are talking about a higher degree of commitment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware that there was hundreds of days in 1995 where General Miletic was signed in as "standing in" for the Chief of Staff on these reports to the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Irregularity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in your view, what practically was General Miletic's position? Was he standing in? Was he replacing? Was it some kind of combination or hybrid of the two?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. He was just replacing the Chief of Staff in his absence. He would have been standing in for him if it hadn't been known where he had gone to and where he would return. The Chief of Staff was at the forward command post where he could be consulted and this Miletic's position meant when the mail came to the staff for the Chief of Staff, then it would arrive at Miletic's desk and he would distribute the mail to whomever it had to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, what the witness still hasn't explained to us is the following: That being a military man, a military officer at the time, one would safely assume that he knew of the difference between replacing and standing in for someone within the military context. If that is so, why -- what prompted him, although he admits now it was a mistake -- what prompted him to choose the latter rather than the former?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That is the ultimate question and I will ask that just that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, we have seen in this case that from early on in July -- excuse me, early on in 1995 and for hundreds of days throughout the year in 1995, General Miletic signed off as standing in. If, like His Honour said, you knew the difference, Miletic knew the difference, the senior staff knew the difference, why is this continued mistake being repeated over and over again all through the year?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Believe me, things started that way and they never changed and why they kept on repeating, I really can't tell you. And you're right, the mistake did repeat, and I don't know why. As a matter of fact, the Chief of Staff was there. He was at the forward command post but he wasn't ill, he wasn't transferred for any length of period. He was healthy. He was at the forward command post. He was performing his job. And the only position that anybody could have was to replace him, not to stand in for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, do you remember that General Milovanovic was actually in command of the Serb forces fighting this massive building front of the Croatian forces? So he had his hands pretty busy at the time, didn't he, as commander of the Serb forces way across the other side of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment before you answer that question. Madam Fauveau? One moment, before you answer that question. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a leading question, very leading even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what's your comment on that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a fact that is in evidence and that what General Milovanovic was doing - and I'm just asking him if that fact kept the -- kept General Milovanovic pretty busy in that Krajina area since this witness would have been in the Crna Rijeka area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But then ask it that way. The way you put it, you haven't really left him any options. You are concluding for him that, of course, that being so, General Milovanovic's hands were pretty busy at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, the witness now has understood what the question is all about and I think he can proceed with his answer straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer that question and I can say that Mr. Prosecutor is absolutely right. Milovanovic had a team and he was really busy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did that -- did that leave his job as Chief of Staff more in the hands of Miletic than it would have had he just been away for an hour or two?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And who was handling the job of chief of operations while Miletic was replacing Milovanovic as the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: In addition to their own duties, the person who replaces the -- their supervisor will also perform the supervisor's duties or the superior's duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who was doing the duties of chief of operations in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment before you answer that question. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that there has been an error in the interpretation. The witness said that in addition to replacing somebody, the person who replaces that other person will also perform his own duties and tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that observation, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Trkulja, do you agree with what Madam Fauveau has just stated? Because if that is so, we need to correct the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that's exactly what I said, and the lady is absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, sir. I think he's answered your last question, irrespective of the fact that I told him to wait, but I think we can move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I think you're correct. I did ask him to try to clarify that, who was doing the job of chiefs of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I believe your answer was Mile; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. My answer was Miletic. Maybe you didn't understand me properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just heard you say Mile and I thought you were referring to him as a nickname. Was that wrong?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Maybe you're right. Miletic, in any case, Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what his nickname is? I mean we obviously know people at your ranks refer to each other as nicknames.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Miletic did not really have any nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But did you say Mile to me earlier?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe the witness already answered this question. I don't see why it is asked of him again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's not waste more time on it, Mr. McCloskey. Please proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So let's start with 11 July, I think as we have before, as you probably recall, this was the day in the afternoon that General Mladic and others were able to walk through Srebrenica. Can you tell us where you were that day, on 11 July?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: In Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what part of the HQ at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Well, it's a command post. The logistical command post, though, was in Han Pijesak. That's where the logistics were. And maybe one thing that should have been the case and wasn't was that personnel people should also have been at the command post. So they were in Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, was there a bomb shelter command post at Crna Rijeka at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes. It's a shelter of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so on the 11th, where were you doing business that day? What building?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: You see, I can't really remember exactly. I know we transferred from the barracks to the shelter but whether it was on the 11th, 12th or the 13th, I can't remember. We were in both those places but I can't recall precisely. It was 12 years ago. I cannot remember. We spent some time in the prefab buildings and we were in the shelter for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember on that day that Srebrenica fell or was liberated that NATO actually made an air attack in the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Based on reports. Otherwise, we wouldn't have known. But we knew from the report that is read every morning before all chiefs of various branches, and that report included the air strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: With air strikes not far away in Srebrenica, does that help refresh your recollection whether you would have been working in the shelter that day or not?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Probably, most probably, looking back I think most probably we were already in the shelter. All I know that is a day or two later, when groups started moving all over the territory, then we moved to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, who do you recall being with you on the 11th, that day that Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: There was Miletic and Sladojevic, I believe, and Pejic did not show up. I cannot be sure about him because he came and went and his office was in Han Pijesak. It was a long time ago. All I know is that he coordinated there. He was in both places. Later, not on the 11th, but later, Sladojevic and Pejic came, and speaking of higher officers, I can't remember who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, do you remember having a chance to look at your previous statement that you -- that you gave on the 11th of July 2005?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you tell me that it was basically correct with some perhaps some "unintelligibles"?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember at the time that you told us that someone else, another senior officer, was with you that day at the command post?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I can't recall precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is an error in the record, if I may assist my colleague, Mr. McCloskey. When the witness was talking about the man who had an office in Han Pijesak but came and went, he said Gvero, but that name is not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's an important observation because what we have in the transcript is Pejic. Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Could you address this issue, Mr. McCloskey, with the witness, please, who has now heard what Mr. Krgovic said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, and Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, colonel, we missed your comment about the whereabouts of General Gvero. Can you tell us where General Gvero was, if you know, on 11 July?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you a specific time line. Whether he came that evening and I played chess with him, whether it was on the 12th, 11th or maybe the 10th, I wouldn't know where he was in the morning because he was assistant commander, and I wouldn't go to his office unless he summoned me. Whether it was on the 11th, on the 12th in the evening, but I know I played chess with him during those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least he's cleared up one side of it. When you were testifying a minute or so ago and you were answering Mr. McCloskey's question as to who you could recall being with you on the 11th, the same day that Srebrenica fell, you mentioned Miletic and Sladojevic as being there with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I said Sladojevic and Pejic came to the Main Staff later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, so it's all wrong. So let's take it one by one. You did mention Miletic. Was he with you on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you mentioned Sladojevic. Was he with you on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you mentioned Pejic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, why did you mention these two persons in answering that question if they were not with you on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they came a day or two later, Pejic and Sladojevic, or maybe I went later with Sladojevic to Srebrenica and visited Crni Vrh. That's why I mentioned them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the same answer to that question, you also mentioned -- you said, "I cannot be sure about him because he came and went and his office was in Han Pijesak." Who had his office in Han Pijesak? Who did you mention as having his office in Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Have I covered the whole territory, Mr. Krgovic and Mr. McCloskey? Or do you wish to add --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's fine, if you think it's fine. If you don't agree then perhaps you can add further questions to it. Yes, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Given he's stated he had a hard time remembering. I think I'd like to refresh his recollection on what he said before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. We are not stopping you. We are just clarifying his previous answer to you because there were at least two mistakes there. As it is, the transcript shows Sladojevic being present on the 11th and Han Pijesak being the place where Pejic had his office when the witness said it was General Gvero who had his office there. Let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, let me -- excuse me, Colonel, let me read back to you what you had told us at the time to see if this refreshes your recollection and it can be found on page 11 of the English and on page 10 and 11 of the B/C/S, and I asked you a question, "Okay, so the attack on Srebrenica took place on 6 July, Srebrenica we know all fell or was liberated, depending on how you look at it, on the 11th of July, and as you know, it's the anniversary of that today and, of course, we've all been hearing about Srebrenica ever since that period of 1995." "So can you tell us where you were during -- doing this day Srebrenica fell on 11 July?" And you say, "Even before the 11th, I was at my command post. So together with Sladojevic, me and this pilot, I think it was Pejic, Pejic was his name, Gvero, Gvero and Miletic too." And then I ask, "General Milan Gvero?" And you say, "Yes, yes, General Milan Gvero." And then we ask, there is a few other questions and I ask you, "Okay. And who again was with you in that area of the command post in Crna Rijeka on 11th?" And you say, "So I just listed the names. Gvero, Miletic, myself, Sladojevic, Pejic. And now I can't remember the -- some lower officers too. It's been a long time."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you answer the question, yes, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, basically I'm not objecting to this line of questioning but the Prosecutor just omitted from this first passage one part and then went on to read the next part which completely changes the sense. The witness there speaks of the logistical command post and the location in Han Pijesak. So he took out of context this statement of the witness because precisely in the part that the Prosecutor omitted, the witness says there is a command post in Han Pijesak and they were there, which completely changes the sense of the whole passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Do you wish to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's absolutely not correct. I'm not changing the context of anything. And he did talk -- he did go on to talk about the other command post but that's why I came back specifically to Crna Rijeka. I can read that. I was just trying to save some time, but given the objection I'll read the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, can I make a suggestion? Instead of my colleague reading this into the transcript, maybe it's better if the witness reads his own text and then my colleague can ask the questions he wants. I think it will be better proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's precisely what we were going to suggest to Mr. McCloskey to do. If you have the version in B/C/S, we can make it available to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And colonel, you can see the orange outline, that's where you first mention Gvero. And then the part that was objected to that I didn't read is the part below that and then shortly after that, you'll see when I get to the specific question and I guess while the witness is reading it, I can read out the part that counsel would like read out as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime, I think if we are to follow properly, Mr. Krgovic's submission and your reaction to it, I think we also we would like to hear read out the content of the missing --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and I can do that and I had just, as I said, I did that to save sometime but I'll do that now. And as you recall, he volunteered that he was with Gvero and Miletic, and then I confirmed General Milan Gvero and I -- and then I say, "And where were you all?" And then he says, "We were all in the command post. Now the staff was divided into two parts so the rear part was in Han Pijesak and the staff-- I mean the command part in Crna Rijeka. Now in Crna Rijeka we had two locations. Those were the barracks and the command post, wartime command post. Now, how can I explain this? Dug up in the ground. So we spent some maybe about 10 days, maybe even more than 10 days, in this command post." And then I say, "Okay. And when Srebrenica fell on the 11th, were you -- where were you?" And the colonel answers, "At that place. And that's where we stayed." And then I say, "In Han Pijesak?" And he says, "No, no, the command post in Crna Rijeka." And then I ask, "Okay. And who again was with you in the area to command post in Crna Rijeka on the 11th?" And that's when he says, "So I just listed the names, Gvero, Miletic, myself, Sladojevic, Pejic and now I can't remember the -- some lower officers too. It's been a long time."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic, I noticed you stand up while Mr. McCloskey was reading. What's your problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's the translation issue because in B/C/S the first sentence looks different, so can I read that in B/C/S to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I think you read it to us for the time being because the witness is being asked questions by Mr. McCloskey. But of course the witness will hear. Yes, if you could read it out, please? Slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "And where were all of you? We were all at the command post, no, not in... because the staff was divided into two segments. The logistical part was in Han Pijesak while the staff, chiefs of branches and the command part, were in Crna Rijeka." So in the first sentence, he says, "We were at the command post," comma, "not in ..." which is unclear. In my opinion, this changes the meaning a bit because this addition "not in" does not exist in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, do you wish to comment on that or should we go straight to the witness who has read what there is in the statement, understands the language and then whatever he says is going to be translated to us in English, hopefully in a correct manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's the better way to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, Colonel Trkulja, you've heard the debate that has been going on between Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Krgovic and ourselves intervening in the meantime. What's your position now that you have read the statement and also heard submissions on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge, if I get specific now, I told you I can't get the date right because Sladojevic and Pejic as soon as they came to the Main Staff, they were assigned to the operations organ. Now, the only problem here is I can't remember whether they arrived on the 9th, on a transfer order, or the 10th or the 11th. But at the time in any case, they were in the operations organ. So practically, the whole problem is the date because as soon as they arrived, they were there. Now, when I was saying this, it was already ten years later. I thought they were there on the 11th when I was giving the interview, because after ten years, I can't remember whether it was on the 11th, the 9th or the 13th. But it seemed to me, since they were already at the command post, that they were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we are definitely talking of Crna Rijeka and not Han Pijesak, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, only about Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Let's -- can you tell us a little bit about how the reports from the Main Staff to the president were compiled, and who compiled and drafted those reports, how were they reviewed by the staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Prosecutor, sir, in July, General Milovanovic took a group away with him and the staff remained with a small number of officers. I as a chief of a branch, wrote up reports but waiting for reports to come in from subordinates. There were six corps and they sent in their reports on two pages each. All this had to be summed up, all those 12 pages had to be summed up on two pages. You looked at those reports and you saw that they contain two pages. So I put in the most important things. Once all these reports came in, I would write it up, send it to be typed up, and then give it to Miletic to sign, and then it would go to filing and the encryption. That's -- that was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And would General Miletic sometimes have changes or alterations to your summaries?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes, not often but sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what would he do if he had changes?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Well, he would cross out a sentence or a word, he would insert the word he thought was better and then he would give it to the typist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's start with one of those documents so we can show the Court how that worked. I'm going to start with a 12 July report, and I don't think I have a B/C/S for you but it will come up on the screen, if I don't. And it is number P02748. And we'll just start-- I'll go over a couple of the key or important parts of the beginning. It's entitled, "The VRS Main Staff," dated 12 July. And then very urgent. To the president of the Republika Srpska. And then it lists the various corps and some other units. Okay. And then as you know, it goes through the various corps and we get to paragraph 6, which is the Drina Corps, but let's flip to the end of this document first so that we can see the signature page. Now, we see Zastupa basically standing in for the Chief of Staff, General Miletic. And the initials are not very clear on this document but if we could blow that up a little bit they are basically R and then the D with a slash in it "Dj," I think. Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: It's not my initials. The Dj can only be Djeric but Djeric was not at the command post so who could it be? He is the only one whose surname begins with the"Dj,", Djeric. It can't be Pejic. It can't be Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: And I know Djeric wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall looking at the same documents from the 10th and the 11th in my office? Do you remember whose initials were on those, the 10th and the 11th, basically the two days before that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I think they were mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. All right. Now, do you know why -- do you know where you were on this day or why your initials aren't on this one on the 12th? Could you have been gone or do you have any memory of that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I wasn't away. It's not like I was designated to write these things constantly. When the officers were present in the operations organ, they would write the reports rather than any chief of branch. Somebody must have come there, I don't know how or why. I was away just for one day and a half in July. I was away from the command post only one day and a half in July. And that's what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to paragraph 6 of this document, which is the Drina Corps section, and it's page 3 in the B/C/S, paragraph 6. We see it's entitled, "The enemy" and the first part of that big paragraph A is talking about areas that I'm not interested in asking you about. But then as we get to the bottom of that, it says, "The enemy has been attempting to withdraw from the Srebrenica enclave with women and children in the direction of Ravni Buljin and Konjevic Polje but ran into a minefield." And then as we get to B, it's the situation of the corps. But before I get to B, this section A, do you have any independent recollection of that information and knowing that information at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I used to read the reports in the morning, but I was aware of what will be put in the report even the evening before, because I was the one who drafted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So at the time you were aware. How about -- how about now all these years later? Do you remember anything about that information now?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I read this report of the Zvornik Brigade for the first time now. I don't know why the supplementary report was not read there. And some things have now become clearer than they were at the time and all this time up to a couple of days ago, when I read this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You say -- can you tell us what reports of the Zvornik Brigade you've read recently in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: The report from Colonel Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember the date of that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: 16 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we are still here, we are not quite to the 16th yet, we are on the 12th in this report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I can't see the date here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah. Just so you know, this is the -- this is the 12th, the report from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Doesn't really matter, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I notice it's break time. It might be a good time to just stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are all here. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, Colonel. I want to just continue briefly to get through this document that's up on the screen. If you could concentrate on that section B, the situation in the corps, and I'll read it briefly and ask you a question or two about some of it. But just before I do, can -- where does the -- can you -- and I think you said this, but can you just clarify where the information that is in this report, where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: All this information, starting with the bullet point A, the 1st Krajina Corps, to the bullet point 6, the Drina Corps, came from the reports of the corps commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there times when information was added to these Main Staff reports that was received over the telephone or in some other reports than the two-page corps report that you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I can claim with certainty, because I drafted these reports, that I never received information over the telephone or in a telegram. The report started at 9.00 onwards, when I awaited information from corps command in order to draft my reports. No additional documents ever made it to the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the general -- or the situation in July, do you remember about what time General Miletic would have reviewed the report and signed off on it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: You see, I can speak in general terms and pinpoint the time. Sometimes corps reports would come late. They should have arrived by 9.00. Still some came at 11.00, half past 11.00. Sometimes I would wake him up at midnight to sign. Sometimes the reports would be drafted by 10.00. Then I would take them to the operations room and he would sign that those reports -- it all depended on the times when the corps reports arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you say 9.00, 10.00 or 11.00, you're talking about in the evening is when the corps reports would come?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about the evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And looking at this section B, entitled, "The situation in the corps," it says, "All the corps units are at the highest level of combat readiness and are doing everything to ensure that there are no surprises." And then it says, "The units engaged in carrying out the Krivaja 95 task are carrying out all the combat tasks according to plan." Do you recall what Krivaja 95 was?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes. It was the operation near Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then it says, "In the course of the day, they liberated the village of Potocari and they are continuing to advance in order to liberate all the places in the Srebrenica enclave." Can you read the next sentence, what -- our English translation is not clear but could you read the next sentence in the report?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: "On the axis, some of our units and MUP units organised ambushes" this is an error in grammar, "in order to destroy Muslim extremists who did not surrender and who are trying to break out from the enclave and proceed towards Tuzla."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for helping us with that. Then the next section is "the situation in the territory," and it says, "In the Drina Corps zone, the population is being taken from Srebrenica enclave to Kladanj in an organised manner." And what population is that, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, can I have the text on the screen? Can this be scrolled up a little? To be very concrete, I can't say anything about this issue because I did not see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Go ahead and take your time from this, see if you can answer my question.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I suppose that it was all the population, but I can't say anything more specific than that. I can't even say that this is correct. I can't, because I was not present. I did not have any further information as to what population was being transported in vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say you weren't present, do you mean you weren't present in -- where these events were happening or you weren't present at the headquarters where the report was being written?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: One can see what is written in the report. However, how things were organised, who was -- who loaded the vehicles, I wasn't there. I am not the right person to tell you how this was all organised, how the whole thing developed. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I wasn't asking you how it was all organised. This information in this report, would that have been information that the people at the headquarters, including yourself, General Miletic, was aware of?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Based on the report that we received from the Drina Corps, this was well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So is the answer yes?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And by sending this report to the president of the Republika Srpska, can you conclude that the people that received this report at the president's office would have knowledge of this information as well?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I think they did. I think so. I can't claim for a fact that they did. But this must have reached the president and the president most probably read this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, was that your expectation in writing these reports from the Main Staff, that they would be read by the president?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Whenever I drafted a report, I always expected that eventually the president would read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at this time period, if it was you and General Miletic and General Gvero at the command post and no other high-ranking soldiers in this time period, who would have been in charge at the command post?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Well, at that time, we only dealt with minor matters. General Miletic would draft letters, and one might say that he was in charge, although he wasn't. The highest-ranking officer and the oldest officer was Gvero. But he only appeared every now and then. Sometimes he would call in the evening to say that he was there, he wanted us to play chess. As for the orders, as for dealing with situations, he wouldn't go into any of that. He would only be present in the morning when the reports were read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. McCloskey. Yes, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have a mistake in the transcript. In last sentence on page 39, the witness said Gvero wasn't present in the morning when the reports were read, whereas in the transcript it says just the opposite, that Gvero was present when the reports were read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, do you agree with what Mr. Krgovic has just corrected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree fully. He was never, all this time, the three years that I was in the Main Staff, he was never present in the morning when the reports were being read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, you just said that General Miletic would draft letters, and one might say that he was in charge, although he wasn't. It's a simple question: Who was in charge in this military command post when it was Miletic, Gvero and yourself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Colonel. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness has never made a basis for that, and maybe somebody else was in charge, maybe Mladic, Tolimir, somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object again to this. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. Please proceed with your answer, Colonel. Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Our objection is that that question mischaracterises the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's precisely what he said earlier on, and Mr. McCloskey is seeking a clarification. Let's go back to the part where the witness -- if you look at line 19 to 21 on page 39, to the answer as who would have been in charge at the command post at a time when there was just the witness, General Miletic and General Gvero at the command post, the witness said, "General Miletic would draft letters and one might say that he was in charge, although he wasn't." Yes, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just read what he had said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let's hear what Madam Fauveau has to say. Go ahead, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am not saying that the witness didn't say this, but what the witness is talking about is the staff of the Main Staff, he's not talking about the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, please, please, please. Let her -- I think we've heard what you had to say. We've heard what you had to say. What you stated earlier on, Colonel, needs some clarification because when you say that he was in charge although he wasn't in charge, you need to explain what you mean by that. Please go ahead with your explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It does seem to me that an explanation is in order. For example, a telegram arrived from the forward command post from General Mladic. It arrives at Miletic's desk with an order as to what needed to be done. Miletic is an operative. He drafts the -- what needed to be drafted. That's why I'm saying that he wasn't in charge because he could not issue any orders or decisions independently. He could not issue orders on his own. He would only follow the instructions from the forward command post, and the commander also gave instructions as to who would sign such orders. Gvero was the oldest, so he was the one who signed those documents. That's why I'm saying that he was there, he was the one who did all that, but that's why there is ambiguity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, who would General Miletic be getting his orders from that he would be passing on?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Exclusively from General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you -- I want to -- you gave us a little bit of a different answer when I asked you that question in the interview. Could you go to what is tab 5 in the little blue -- blue tabs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, can you assist the witness, just in case he cannot follow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You should see a tab 5 in the blue part. It's page 12 of the English. It's about the same page. And I asked you, on 20 -- line 24 in the English, "Okay. And this small group you've described, who was in charge?" And you say, "Gvero was the most senior one, but in reality, Miletic was ... was the one." And then there is something that's unintelligible. Do you remember telling that to me?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm repeating it again now. And what I've just said to the Judge is that. He didn't -- was not in charge of anything. He was just reading the telegrams that arrived and so on and so forth. I'm not changing anything with regard to what is written in here, that you have just quoted from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's keep going in this, just keep reading a bit. It's on page 13, and I ask, "Okay. All right. And tell us about what you remember about the day Srebrenica fell. What kind of work did you and others do?" And you say, "So we -- we got an assignment from Miletic." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Well, we received -- I can't see it in here. Mr. Prosecutor, what you've just quoted, I can't find it in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need some assistance here, someone could direct us to the corresponding page in B/C/S. We should still be behind tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Colonel, we flipped to the wrong page. It's page 12 in the B/C/S and we've got it outlined there for you.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does that help? Did you get an assignment?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I did. But not just me. We all did. We took turns at the command to see whether the security was in place, in order to prevent any unpleasant surprises. We would take turns to leave the shelter and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who did you get that assignment from?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: From Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was Mladic present the when Miletic gave you that assignment?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. I suppose that the assignment had been conveyed by him over the telephone, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this assignment, as you have stated, was to look after the security of the headquarters of the VRS command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this was a very important assignment, I take it? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a form --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This seems like a benevolent question but still a very leading one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's asking him whether it was an important assignment or not. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was going in the leading direction and I tried to save it at the end with a yes or no, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. McCloskey, and he's answered it anyway, I think, although no, it's not in the transcript. So Colonel, you need to answer the question again. And Mr. McCloskey --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was just a formality because the security also had been given their task, to be alert. It was a formality for us because they were always on the detail, on the security detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had the command post been overrun by Muslim forces, that would have been a real disaster, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I don't think so. Because the command post was well secured. There were mines placed all around. There were guards on various axes. I don't think it would have been. But just in case, the security propositions were in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was this an order you received from General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: One can't say that this was an order. It was just an instruction according to which we divided ourselves into twos. We would spend an hour outside. We would then be replaced by the other pair. There was nothing written to that effect, nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when General Miletic, who has the direct line of communication from Mladic, issues a colonel an instruction to look into the security of the command post, it's not an order, in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Well, we didn't go out to really do anything. We just went out to see whether the guards were in place, that they were awake, that they were not slacking at what they were doing. This is what we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, that's not an answer to the question that was put to you. The question was a very simple one, whether these -- this assignment that, the way it has been translated to us, whether you consider that to be an order, and if you don't consider it to be an order, why don't you consider it to be an order or what distinction are you making in your mind between that assignment and an order? This is what Mr. McCloskey is basically asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a matter of fact, there is no difference between an order and an assignment, because both had to be carried out. We would go out. We did the same as if we had been ordered to do that. There is no major difference. This is something that we carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Did you receive an order from General Miletic to go somewhere in those days?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Sladojevic and I were ordered to go to the Zvornik Brigade and to convey a message that the security of the units on the front line should be raised to the highest level because there was a possibility that Muslim groups would come from Srebrenica on their way to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did General Miletic give you this order, as best as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Look here, after the 11th, when I provided my first statement in which I said that it was in the morning, I gave it a long and hard thought. You were the one who put me that question, whether it was in the morning or in the evening, and I said that it was in the morning. However, later on, it occurred to me that this was not in the morning but in the evening. He also arranged for the transportation. So that a vehicle was awaiting us in the morning. My first, my initial answer was given in haste. When I said that this was in the morning, I was wrong. It occurred later to me. I remembered only later that it was actually in the evening but I don't think it makes any difference, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We just need your best recollection. And do you remember roughly how many days after Mladic had gone through Srebrenica you got this order from General Miletic? Or if you know the date?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Look here, I've told you that already, the last time I spoke to you, I told you, I had it in subconscious and I went through the reports to look for it. It seemed to me at the time and it still seems to me that this was maybe three or four days after the fall of Srebrenica. If you look at the reports, it seems that this was on the 15th or the 16th. This is when I looked at Pandurevic's report. In my recollections, that was not the case, but it seems that it actually was, if you look at the report, but, you know, it was a long time ago, 12 years ago, and it's very difficult for me to remember the exact dates of any of the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fair enough. How, in what manner or form, did General Miletic give you this order? Written, verbal?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Verbally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Face to face, over the telephone? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: In the operations room. My rest room was just next to the operations room. He would call me, tell me the assignment, to raise the readiness of the Zvornik Brigade units on the front line. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this in the -- in the bunker or above ground?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in the bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was it in person or over the phone? That wasn't clear.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: In person, in person. We were both there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was there anybody else in the room that you remember when he gave you this order?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as best as you can remember, can you tell us what he said to you, what Miletic said to you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I'll tell you what I remember. The assignment was as I said before, and he told us to drop by the command of the Drina Corps to pick up the senior officer and to tour the front line, and to drop by the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So the -- when you say the command of the Drina Corps, that would be the HQ in the city -- sorry, let me finish, it will be clear. When you say the command of the Drina Corps, you mean the headquarters in the city of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you say that you now remember receiving that order on the eve -- on an evening a few days after the fall of Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, prior to receiving that order, either that day that you received it or the day before, had you been in the field anywhere?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. In the whole month of June, I was away from the command only for a day and a half. That was that day when I left and I returned the next day after lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We got the translation of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I want him to clarify. Is this June or July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] July, July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what was that day in July that you left? Was that before or after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: After the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So if Srebrenica fell on the 11th of July and you got ordered a few days after to go to Vlasenica, it was between the fall of Srebrenica and when you got ordered to go to Vlasenica that you left and had gone out somewhere; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. When I got the orders, in the evening, I left for Vlasenica the next morning, picked up one officer, one major, to take us to the Zvornik Brigade, and from there to the front line, and before that he asked me to drop by Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.
