We'll get to that, but what I'm asking you to clarify is in one answer, when I asked you if you'd been to the field, you said, "In the whole month," meaning July, "I was away from the command only for a day and a half. That was the day when I left. And I returned the next day after lunch." And you just told me that day you left was after the fall of Srebrenica. That's what you've testified to. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, are you talking about this trip to Zvornik as the day and a half that you were away from the command post or is there something in addition to that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. That's that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Aside from to secure the lines, did you have any other information on what this trip to the Zvornik Brigade was all about?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: It was exclusively to raise the alertness and the security of the units on the front line, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you given any information on why Vinko Pandurevic needed to be reminded to raise his alertness?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Vinko Pandurevic was busy, engaged by the commander of the Drina Corps. Only his deputy was there, the Chief of Staff, Obrenovic. Why Miletic told us to go to the Zvornik Brigade, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And tell us what you did the next day, in the morning. I think you were starting to tell us about following that order.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Well, that morning, Sladojevic and I got into a car with a driver. We stopped by the command. There is a parking lot there. We didn't even park, because a major was already waiting for us. It's not Lazic. Lazic is an operative. Some colonel or a major. I can't remember his name to this day. To take us to the front line. Later when you ask me, I'll explain. So when we were going from Vlasenica, Sladojevic asked me, "Come on, please, there is so much talk about Srebrenica, let's go and see it." So we toured about half of the town, never leaving the car, before we left for Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clear up something, you said when you went to the -- you stopped by the command, there was a parking lot, was that the command of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm only talking about Vlasenica because I never went to the forward command post, and when I speak, I never refer to the forward command post. I mean the stationary command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had you been to the Vlasenica command post the day before?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. Only that morning, to pick up that officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did that officer get in the car with you and go?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as you sit here now, do you know if it was a major or a colonel? I think you've said both. You're not sure?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I'm certain that a colonel was awaiting for us and then summoned a major who got into the car and then we continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does the name Colonel Cerovic -- I think I've asked you before but does Cerovic - you've had a chance to think about it - could that have been -- does that sound familiar?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No, it doesn't ring a bell. Maybe I saw that man. Maybe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And after your tour of Srebrenica, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: To Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And roughly what time of day did you get to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I think it was lunchtime, around 12.00, maybe later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where in Zvornik did you go?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: To the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see anybody there?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No one but the duty officer. That major spoke to him and explained to him what and where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you mean, "what and where"?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Where the officers, the senior officers, were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you have any recollection of that duty officer, who that was, what rank, anything about him?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I know that it was a reserve officer, not active-duty, but I can't be sure whether he was a captain or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And after getting these instructions or whatever it was you got, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: The major -- in fact, I showed the major which part of the front line I wanted to visit, and he knew all the by-roads. When you turn away from Zvornik, we went to that location. Once there, I ran into Obrenovic, who was close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say you showed the major which part of the front line you wanted to visit, how did you know what part you wanted to visit?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I showed randomly that location, because I didn't know anything about it, and then it turned out it was interesting. Nobody told me at the corps command where to go and even the duty officer didn't tell me anything. I just pointed randomly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did you -- what area of this battlefield did you randomly point to?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Well, where the Muslim group tried to break out through our lines and move towards Tuzla. I hadn't known about it, and at the brigade command, they hadn't known about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, how did you know to go to this area of the breakout?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: By accident. I could have pointed out another location, but I pointed my finger at random there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was that? Do you know the name of the place?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I think it was elevation Crni Vrh. There must be another place name but I can't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened when you got there?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: As soon as the vehicle stopped, Obrenovic turned up from God knows where, and he reported to me that a Muslim formation had started to move around 5.000 people, that they ran into mortars, they were massacred, they ran into self-propelled vehicles, like tanks, and he tried using those self-propelled vehicles like tanks to push them back, and that he had established contact with the leader of that group and agreed that he would separate two platoons, in fact, to withdraw two platoons, from the front line, that they will de-mine 600 to 1.000 metres of a belt from the front line, and that they would be able to pass through that corridor the next day around 11.00 or 12.00. He reported that to me and then Colonel Lazic, an operations officer at the Drina Corps, turned up. Now, I'm not sure whether Vinko Pandurevic appeared at that moment or not. I'm sure he was there the next day. But while this was going on, it was already getting dark. Maybe not dark but it was late afternoon. I'm not sure whether Vinko was there then, but he was certainly there the next morning. He sat next to me on that elevation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did Major Obrenovic, in this briefing to you, tell you anything about Serb casualties?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. He still had not received the numbers. The events were still fresh. He knew only about the mortars and the self-propelled tanks. But he had not received information from his subordinated units. He just told me about the mortars and the tanks he used. He knew there were losses but he didn't know how many. So he didn't tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When he told you about opening this line to allow people to pass, did he indicate he had the authority of his commander to do that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Prosecutor, sir, when you showed me that report three days ago, and when I read the report of Colonel Pandurevic, and when I replayed this whole movie as to what Obrenovic told me, I can now say with 90 per cent certainty, although I told you at the time it was only Obrenovic, after seeing the report, I see that Pandurevic was actually justifying himself, so I now believe that Vinko Pandurevic was the one who ordered that this line be opened. He didn't mention women, children and unarmed people because the report is contradictory. It was Vinko who must have ordered the elite unit of the 28th Srebrenica Division and Vinko, I am certain, 90 per cent, although it's not written anywhere, was the one who ordered it, because that report was not a situation report. It was his justification, self justification, before the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And let's just so we are clear, we are talking about the interim combat report of 16 July 1995. It's 65 ter 330. And that was among the many documents you were provided to help refresh your recollection of these events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes. And thank you for showing it to me because I had not read that report at the command post. I saw it then for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. How long did you stay out in that area that you've gone to and seen at least Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Obrenovic, Lazic and some other officers. I can't remember the names of the Drina Corps. I saw them for the first time. They introduced themselves but still it was 12 years ago. Lazic found us accommodation for the night in a monastery. We spent the night there, we had breakfast in the morning and we -- this passage was supposed to start at 10.00. We came there earlier. Now I'm sure Vinko Pandurevic was there. He sat next to me. There was Lazic. There was this major, Sladojevic. There were certainly around 10 officers. We were sitting at an elevation. I didn't have these glasses with me. And I couldn't see through the hedge how they were withdrawing because these are reading glasses only, and I heard from them that the people were passing but basically I didn't see them. And we kept sitting there until he got the report that the last person had passed through. When that happened, it was ordered that the soldiers come back to the front line and close this line. Now, whether I was still with Lazic, I don't remember. In any case, we returned from there to Crna Rijeka. They reported verbally to Miletic -- we reported verbally to Miletic, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When Miletic had given you this order you now remember being an evening, was Mladic present anywhere in the area of the bunker, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: You see, throughout this time that we were in that shelter, I'm sure about one occasion that Mladic came by. He didn't stay long. He may have come twice. I'm sure about only once. He didn't stay long. He just toured the command, the operations room, had a look, and then left. In all that time, he visited once or twice. I'm not sure about twice but I'm sure about once. The second time, I recollect very vaguely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So can you give us any idea where he -- where Mladic was when Miletic gave you this order to go to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Probably at the forward command post, together with Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This small group, you, Sladojevic, who was in charge of your small group?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you got back to Crna Rijeka, who reported back to General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you report to him? Can you just give us your best recitation of what you remember?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Sir, everything that I've just told you was the same thing I said to Miletic. That we had passed through Srebrenica, that we visited the Zvornik Brigade, from the point the major joined us to when we met with Obrenovic, what Obrenovic told us about the mortars and the rest, about the decision to let this group pass through towards Tuzla. I reported all that to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you give him your viewpoint on the decision to allow the Muslim group to pass through?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: To be quite frank, as soon as Obrenovic reported to me that he had agreed with the Muslims that he would let them through, since I was occupying the post I was occupying, I immediately realised, although I didn't want to say anything, that it was not a decision Obrenovic should have made or made. It must have been a decision of Vinko Pandurevic. To open up a line in the front line, 600 to 1.000 metres, it was something that only the commander could have decided. It's not something the Chief of Staff can decide. Obrenovic didn't decide that. I'm certain about that because God knows how many brigades could have passed through that corridor. And when I saw that report, which seems to be in contradiction with the other report, that was something that the commander decided himself without the knowledge of the commander of the Main Staff or the Drina Corps, because he could have destroyed those forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And again you're talking -- when you say report, you're talking about the interim combat report from the brigade to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, and to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were there. How -- and you've just concluded that Pandurevic could have destroyed those forces. Can you explain how he could have done it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: It was extremely simple and easy. Srebrenica had fallen. He had those forces. He could have engaged some units using mortars, recoilless guns and others to destroy them. They were in a depression, these people. Nobody would have survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you report your opinion, that opinion, to General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. I only conveyed what Obrenovic told me without stating my personal opinion, but the report you showed me convinced me in my earlier suspicion, and I now believe that what I had only suspected then is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you get a written order, ever get any kind of a written order, to go to Zvornik on this trip you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing this written order signed by Mladic dated the 17th of July, ERN 00922973?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: In 2005, I saw it, when you showed it to me in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That was the first time you had ever seen that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: That's when I saw it, and then I told you that I did not go pursuant to that order. I had already been and returned when that order came containing certain tasks that I wasn't aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, we heard from another witness in the case that the trip to Srebrenica was done after you visited the lines in Zvornik. Do you think that -- you could have got that mixed up or do you think you're right, that you went to Srebrenica before you visited the lines in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I'm sure. When I picked up major in Vlasenica, Sladojevic asked me, and it had never occurred to me before, he asked me to go and look at that place, Srebrenica, and then I asked the driver to make a turn there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, there is an intercept I want to show you. It's an intercept you've seen before and we've talked about before, and it's-- we'll show you the original version of it, which is 1187B, which should come up on your screen. A is the English version. So this is a conversation that we believe the Muslim army intercepted. And it is thought to be intercepted on the 16th of July at 11.11 hours in the morning, between Colonel Ljubo Beara, person named Cerovic and a person identified as X. Now, if you could -- I know you've seen this before but take a look at it. And perhaps we can allow him to see the whole document. I have a photocopy, but I think -- can you read that okay, Colonel? Maybe they can bring it up a little better.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First of all, who is Colonel Ljubo Beara?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: He was the security officer in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know a Colonel Cerovic of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No, and I don't even know what position he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you can see, and I won't read it all, but we can see that in the early part of this there is some talk about triage. Triage has to be done on the prisoners is mentioned by Cerovic. And someone X says that Colonel Beara is right here by me. Cerovic says, "Give me Beara." Then there is a short conversation between Cerovic and Beara. And once Cerovic gets connected with Beara, Cerovic says, "Trkulja was here with me just now and he was looking for you. I don't know." Now, do you know of any other officers of the Main Staff or the Drina Corps named Trkulja?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. No, I was the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And according to this, if Cerovic was at the headquarters of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica, he's stating that you were just there meeting with him. Did you around this time period you're talking about meet with a person named Cerovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: A colonel was waiting for me there. He may have been Cerovic but I never exchanged a single sentence with me. The only thing I told him or asked him, rather, was who was going to come with me. That was all. And I never left the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you were in Vlasenica, at the headquarters, as you've told us you were, had you received instructions from the Main Staff to pass on to the Drina Corps that triage must be done on the prisoners over in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. Not a word was said about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Now, let's just go through the estimates. We have a revision of the given estimates for cross-examination. Mr. Zivanovic, you had asked for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ostojic, you had asked for 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think 20 to 30 minutes may suffice but I'll look at it again but no more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Bourgon? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have two questions for the witness and no more than ten minutes at the most. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. And Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. We will not have any questions for this witness, just as we had announced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Fauveau? You had asked for an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I believe that one hour will suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, less than 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 15 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Who wishes to go first? Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, when examined by the Prosecutor in 2005, or when interviewed, rather, you said that General Milovanovic was the closest to General Mladic and that he was the most competent officer. Can you confirm that today? Can you confirm that General Milovanovic was the most competent officer and the closest to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Just one correction in terminology. He was the most professional and skillful one. And that's what I can confirm today.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And he was also his closest associate?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: He was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When General Miletic replaced General Milovanovic, he could never replace him as a deputy commander would?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No, he only replaced him within the framework of the staff partially because he could not issue any orders to anybody. This was not within his purview. He was just a deputy. He was not the acting commander, standing in for the commander, and only such people could actually exercise command.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that General Miletic was not General Mladic's adviser?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In your interview with the representative of the Prosecutor's Office, you said on page 40, which is 38 in B/C/S, that General Miletic was from the rocket unit. What exactly did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: This is the anti-aircraft defence, long-range. He did not complete the military academy in Belgrade, but in Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In Zadar, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I believe that Miletic as an operative could put some thesis on the paper when instructions were being given. Mladic would listen to him, just as a formality. But the only person who could help him in professional sense was General Milovanovic and no other.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just one clarification, sir, because the interpretation wasn't finished. You said that General Miletic did not complete the military academy of the army in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: That's true. He completed the military academy in Zadar, which was the anti-aircraft orientation, so he was not the graduate of the ground forces academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You have just spoken about the guards that were organised around the command post. Is it true that such guard posts existed throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes. It is the same security. The only difference was that we had to be extra alert. All the guards had already been explained what the situation was all about, and they knew what to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So this was not a measure that was put in place as an extraordinary measure, in light of the Srebrenica operation?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. The security measures were not stepped up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to give you an indication, instead of having the break at 12.30, we'll have the break at 12.20, ten minutes earlier, all right? So that you regulate your questions accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that the security around the Main Staff facility fell under the staff of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: The Protection Regiment was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You have told us earlier today that the staff of the Main Staff did not have a lot of men on board. Is it true that since there were not enough officers, that you helped General Miletic in the operations room?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I drafted reports, and as for the minor matters that came from above, Miletic carried those out on its own -- on his own.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that the operation that was carried out had not been planned in the Main Staff, according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I, as the chief of a branch, did not know what was going on until the reports started pouring in and I believe that the same is true of the other officers. If the operation had been planned in the Main Staff a map would have had to been drawn in the operations room. It could not have been done in Miletic's room because Miletic's office was too small. Irrespective whether this was done in the barracks or in the shelter, the situation would have been the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In any case, what you are saying is that if that map had been drawn at the Main Staff, you would have seen it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: All the officers of the Main Staff would have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You have also spoken about the reports that arrived at the Main Staff from the corps. Is it true that the Main Staff received reports from the corps but not from the brigades?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: There is a hierarchy. The brigades sent their reports to the corps, the corps drafted their compound reports. They then send those reports to us. And then we forwarded those reports higher up. There is a hierarchy in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In other words, the information that the Main Staff received with regard to the situation on the front line in Eastern Bosnia arrived exclusively from the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes. Everything arrived from the Drina Corps, save for the extraordinary report that was drafted by Pandurevic on the 16th, but I believe that it was their command that didn't want to make any alterations but sent it directly to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show the witness Exhibit number P330, which I believe is the -- precisely this report from the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, did you have in mind this report of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, the one dated 16 of July. You see that this was submitted to the Drina Corps and the Drina Corps received a -- sent this report in its original to the Main Staff without making any alterations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But you have also told us that you never saw this report until the day it was shown to you by the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I suppose that Miletic also didn't want to make any alterations, because I had already sent my main report --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just a moment, sir. Just a moment, sir. This report, the one that you see in front of you, it was sent to the command of the Drina Corps, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And nothing in this report indicates that it might have been sent to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: That's true, but most probably it was sent to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, is this the convenient time for our break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, and thank you, Madam Fauveau. We'll reconvene in 25 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, we were talking about that report that was transmitted to the Main Staff by the corps. Is it true that the officers in the brigade did not address directly the officers and generals in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, they did not. Except in exceptional situations. I believe that this report was sent by the Main Staff after all, in view of certain elements.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm asking not about reports but about telephone calls, for instance.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No, they did not address themselves directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: My colleague tells me that just a moment ago when you were talking at line 16 to 18, you said that it was the Drina Corps that would have sent to the Main Staff the report of the Zvornik Brigade. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So the brigade itself could not have done it on its own, could not have sent it directly?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. It went through the Drina Corps. They didn't change anything. They just sent it on.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the Witness P48? It's a report of the Main Staff dated 14 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you see it's marked here as being sent to the President of Republika Srpska, but also to the commands of various corps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at the heading. This document was typed up at the Main Staff. This document I'm seeing on the screen now was typed at the Main Staff of the VRS and it is filed under a certain number, 03/3-195.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And it was sent to the President of Republika Srpska and also to the commands of various army corps?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And we see that it was sent to the forward command post 2 of the Main Staff of the army, and that's the forward command post where General Milovanovic was located, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness the last page of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We see initials NT. They are yours, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And a moment ago, we saw initials NDj. Could they have been the initials of Mihajlo Djurdjevic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Initials MDj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly, possibly, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you remember the post of Mihajlo [Realtime transcript read in error "Djordjevic"] Djurdjevic at that time, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: He was chief of engineering in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can I just correct, it's page 67, 6, it's Mihajlo Djurdjevic spelled as Dju -- and the rest is correct. Can we say that it was common practice for persons who participated in the drafting of a document to be indicated on reports of the Main Staff like by initials in your case?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: It was not only practice, it was also a rule, according to instructions, for the initials of the person who participated in the drafting and even typing to be indicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So in fact, the full name of the person who wrote the report is written there, not only the initials.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness P5? In B/C/S, it will be page 21. In English, it's 15. Can we zoom in on the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You see it's indicated here that this document was authored by Colonel Radivoje Miletic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the role of Radivoje Miletic in the drafting of this document?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: If you allow me, I'll explain, but it will take time. When the inner circle of the command meets, the operations officer also comes along, although he doesn't belong in the inner circle. When various commands or directives are issued, this operations officer receives instructions, and that's the answer to all the questions that he has to compose, and when he receives this from the commander, he goes back to his office and drafts this. There is a rule governing this, and that rule says that the person who actually wrote this up has to be indicated and the typist as well. The Chief of Staff, who was present at the meeting, reviews the document and checks whether everything was done in the spirit of the instructions given by the commander. If there are any corrections to be made, they are made. But the operations officer is actually a notary in this story. It's taken back to the Chief of Staff and at this point it has already been through two revisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you speak of the chief of the Main Staff, you speak of General Milovanovic in this case, March 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes. In this case, it was Milovanovic. But I said that it was generally the rule according to the instructions for the work of Main Staffs, the operations officer writes this up and hands it in to the Chief of Staff. In this case, it was Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you page 23 now. In English it's strangely page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the signature?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you worked for a long time with General Milovanovic. You recognise the signature of General Milovanovic on this directive 7, what is practically the transmission of directive 7 to the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Well, it's written there, Milovanovic, and the signature is Milovanovic's.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You spoke of meetings that took place in the HQ of the Main Staff every morning. Is it the case that these were meetings of officers who were there at the HQ of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I didn't understand the first part of your question. Morning briefings were?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The morning briefings where reports from various corps were read and analysed, these meetings were attended by officers who belonged to the headquarters of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes. Only organs of the Main Staff were present, nobody else, not politicians, not logistical officers, nobody from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And just to clarify, assistant commanders did not attend these briefings?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that at the barracks in Crna Rijeka, and in the bunker there, General Miletic had his own room?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that General Miletic sent you to Zvornik. Could we say that General Miletic, in fact, conveyed to you an order that only the commander, General Mladic, could have issued?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Zvornik Brigade, you did not have the authority to issue any orders to the officers of the Zvornik Brigade, did you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No, I did not. That's why I only listened and kept my opinion to myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And General Miletic did not have such authority either. He could not give any orders to officers of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, same as me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mean that there were no orders?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: He did not have the authority, the powers.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you came back from Zvornik, you reported to General Miletic, and you spoke at length about what you actually said to him. But did you say that a column of Muslims was actually enabled to pass through by the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I told him absolutely everything. I described to the Prosecutor the whole thing and I can repeat it from my meeting with Obrenovic to the very end. I said exactly the same thing to Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that General Miletic was neither surprised nor concerned that this column of Muslims was able to pass through?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. He took it as a matter of course, something normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that according to the information that the officers in the HQ of the Main Staff at Crna Rijeka had, the civilian population from Srebrenica who wanted to leave could be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only information available to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you had no information from the HQ of the Main Staff about any mistreatment or abuse during this evacuation?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. Out of those people who were there at the command post, nobody had a clue about that. And I don't even know if there was any mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you say, "Over there at the command post," you meant the command post of the Drina Corps, there, on site?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. I mean the command post of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: All right. So what you mean is that nobody at the command post of the Main Staff had a clear idea of what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That calls for a conclusion he cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your comment on that, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe the witness has already answered. I wanted only to clear up what is already on record, but I have no problem stopping there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, it's about line 1 on page 71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We agree with you, Madam Fauveau, on line 2 of page 71, the witness said nobody had a clue about that, so your subsequent question is perfectly in order. If you could answer it, please, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already answered. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It's in fact my mistake because I followed the interpretation in three languages. Could you just tell me, when you say that nobody at the command post had a clear idea what was going on, you mean the command post at Crna Rijeka, the command post of the Main Staff at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout, when I say command post, I mean only the command post of the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I've got only one question left. When you were giving that interview to the Office of the Prosecutor, you said you did not recall the name Krivaja. Is it true that this name was not mentioned at the HQ of the Main Staff before the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. Who is going next? I suggest either the Gvero team or the Beara team. Unless, of course, there is an understanding or an arrangement amongst you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I don't want to interfere with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, my name is John Ostojic and I represent Mr. Ljubisa Beara here. I would just like, if we could look again at document 1182 which was shown to you during your direct examination? 1187, that's correct. While that's being brought up, sir, you remember you gave actually two interviews to the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Peter McCloskey, correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the second interview was a follow-up interview on some documents but it doesn't relate to this exhibit that we are looking at. During your first interview with him, I think he asked you about this exhibit 1187, correct, which as we called it, a purported intercept from July 16th at 11.11 hours. And that was the only time he asked you about that intercept, correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think he asked me about it the second time, just the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that's in dispute. In fact, we have it. It was a short interview and there is no doubt that he didn't ask you about it in the second interview, but if you'd like, I can share that with you but I don't think it's important. My question, sir, is do you remember when you gave this interview to Mr. McCloskey on the 11th of July 2005 and when he asked you about this intercept where your name purportedly is mentioned, you answered him as following and it's on page 41 line 19, when he asked you about whether or not you were looking for someone, and your answer was, first of all, "First of all, I never -- I never asked to see or talk to Beara or Beara." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As you sit here today although it's been a couple of years since your interview, it's still correct, sir, that you never asked to see or to talk to Mr. Beara as seemingly reflected in this purported intercept; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Correct. I didn't ask for that. And I was surprised in 2005 when I saw this document, because I said I had never gotten out of the car, nor did I know the man who was expecting me at Vlasenica. I only asked for an officer to be seconded to me who would take me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I know we have heard Mr. McCloskey's view of who this Cerovic might be, but do you remember a person by the name of Keserovic as well, with a K?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: The name could only be Keserovic, certainly not Cerovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Mr. Ostojic. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the record if we could get the spelling of Keserovic correct, because it does cause confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure. I would rather -- I -- if there is a name you're suggesting, which you think is or may be different from what the witness said, then you please spell it out. If you think it's the same, then we can ask the witness to spell it out and then you can confirm whether it's the same one or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know, so I'll just ask the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you -- if you would be kind enough just to spell the name of this Colonel or Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: He wasn't a colonel, if that's the man I mean. If that's the Keserovic whom I know, because he had served in Macedonia and we had known each other for a long time, I believe he was Lieutenant-Colonel and I can spell his name for you: K-e-s-e-r-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And as you sit here is it -- am I correct that you do not know of any individual named Cerovic, which is C-e-r-o-v-i-c as reflected on this Exhibit 1187; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: You're right, because the Drina Corps did not have units up to establishment so I avoided going there because I would have had to do Miletic's job and tour the infantry. Apart from Lazic, Krstic and Zivanovic, I don't know any other officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, that's all I have with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. I have got Nikolic, Gvero and Pandurevic left. Yes, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have roughly half an hour left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On behalf of General Gvero's defence, I'm going to ask you a few questions about your testimony today. Since the two of us speak the same language I would kindly ask you to wait for the end of my question before starting to give your answer in order to help the interpreters interpret your words and in order to avoid overlapping. In answering Mrs. Fauveau's questions you said that the operation around Srebrenica was not planned or carried out within the Main Staff. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor in his interview asked you and suggested to you that Mladic was in command of that operation and that in the field he was assisted by General Gvero, to which you said this was not true, and that the operation Srebrenica was not executed at the Main Staff. Do you adhere by that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, I adhere by that because this is exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Also, you will remember the discussion about the location of Gvero's office in Han Pijesak and I'm now going to show you a document that concerns the barracks that you have not mentioned in your testimony. One of the previous witnesses has already spoken about this sketch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown P02828?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And please slow down, both of you, witness and Mr. Krgovic. You're not allowing a small pause between question and answer, which is necessary for the interpreters to be able to translate everything to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, this here is the facility in which you were, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I need your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it okay now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is. Can the usher please explain the witness how to use the marker pen, as I'm going to be asking the witness to mark certain places on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you see the facility here. Could you please tell us -- yes. As far as I can understand the correction reads Tolimir which means that he was using two offices at the time. When the blue salon was built, I understand that Gvero no longer had an office in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Sir, I have made a correction here. The blue salon, Tolimir had two rooms because he was with his wife, and then there were the chief of engineers, Salapura, Beara and finally Colonel Maric. The schematic representation on the other side is also wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where your office was?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I can, if you scroll up a little. Here is the operations room and then below it you'll find my office. Can this be scrolled up a little? But this is also incorrect on the left. Above the operations room there should be Miletic, which does not exist here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please make the markings, the necessary markings?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can we scroll up a little?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, if we could, then we would be able to see my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we can do that. So we need to mark this, save it, and then do it again. Yes. And what Judge Kwon is suggesting is also possible. We could scrap this, zoom out a little bit, and then possibly try to get everything done in one, whichever you prefer, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we should do the latter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should start all over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is no big deal. We can scrap this and if the other alternative is not possible, then we can come back to this. All right. So now if we can zoom out on this, please. All right. If you could zoom in just one degree only, please? Okay, and scroll it a little bit down. Okay. Is that okay for your purposes, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So then you can proceed once more with the series of questions to the witness and he will mark the diagram that we have here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Put just a T.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: M stands for Miletic, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's all right, but we haven't got a confirmation on the transcript as to what stands for what. If we start with the first column on the left, M stands for what, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first two offices belong to the chief of staff, Milovanovic. The next, the third office, was Miletic's office. And then after that, the operations room. After the operations room, you can see my room. It was first Djapa and then Djeric's room. And then there was the IT room for computer operators and the toilet. On the right-hand side, the blue room, Tolimir had two offices after the blue room, and after Tolimir was the chief of artillery and engineers, then Salapura, then Beara, the late Maric and Pancic. Those were the only offices that existed in this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the first on the left where you see Miletic's name, Miletic wasn't there, was he? Below Mladic and Milovanovic you see Miletic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. This is just a random marking. There were doors leading from one to another. The second one was General Milovanovic's bedroom and behind there was Miletic's office, which you can't see here, and then the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I will no longer need this diagram but before, can you please put your initials on the diagram and put today's date? You can put it in the right upper hand corner.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On the document, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: What's the date today?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The 10th. 10 September 2007.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'll take you back to another topic that you have already spoken about earlier. It concerns your very brief stay in Srebrenica, when you stopped there on the way to Zvornik. You had an occasion to pass through the town of Srebrenica on your way to the Zvornik sector?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice at the time, in Srebrenica, can you describe, as far as we could see, there is just one long street with flanked by houses on both sides?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, but more to the left, as you look from the direction of Bratunac, on the right-hand side there are houses missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice, at the time, any traces of shells or damaged roofs or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: As we were entering Srebrenica and as we turned around in the centre, we could not see even a tile on the roof missing. People were cleaning their courtyards but they were getting rid of rubbish and garbage, nothing else. There were no traces of any damaged walls or debris.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just one thing. When you were talking about the left side full of houses and on the right side some houses missing, you meant that there had been no houses there in the first place?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No, because there was a ditch or a canal there, just in one part of that street on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You are an expert in artillery and armoured vehicles. Did Srebrenica at the time look at you as a town which had been shelled for days?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Srebrenica looked like no shell had ever fallen on it. If there had been shelling at least one roof would have been damaged and I didn't see any such thing. I went from the north to the south and back and I didn't see any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that was your impression that you conveyed when you arrived back at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, now I'm going to move on to another topic. In answering the Prosecutor's question about General Gvero and his role, you said that when you returned from the Zvornik sector, that Gvero wasn't there because Gvero did not interfere in the staff matters. Would you confirm that today?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: That was the case, so I have to confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And furthermore, when you were asked by the Prosecutor about Gvero's position and what he did, you said that Gvero was in charge of the signals centre and information centre, he published wall papers and he was more or less engaged in the matters of morale. Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you can confirm this as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to belittle his role but that was his only job and that's the only thing that he could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the transcript, we are missing one word. I said wall paper, i.e. the bulletin that is usually pinned to a notice board in military barracks to inform soldiers of what -- of what's going on, and this is missing in the transcript. Would you agree with me that this is what you said to the Prosecutor and would you confirm that today?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In answering the Prosecutor's question who asked you about the influence of certain officers and their significance in the Main Staff, he -- the Prosecutor also asked you about the influence that General Gvero had on the command. Do you remember what you said to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Well, I can't quote myself, but when it came to the use of the units, I believe that Gvero did not have a say in that. He was in charge of morale, and in his previous career, he was only a platoon commander, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you a passage from your interview with the Prosecutor. You said at the time that, if you -- this is page 36 of the B/C/S version, and in English I have a redacted version so if you can just bear with me, this is page 40. You said at the time you can look at somebody's CV. Gvero cannot have any influence. Gvero could not have any influence given the fact that all his life he was the principal of a military grammar school. He was never in command of any military unit so what proposal could he have put forth?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: That is the case. That indeed was the case. I can't change anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There is a translation issue. It says does not have much influence and I don't know if the booth can have the English so they can read from it in this situation to try to avoid -- I know it's difficult but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The difference is between "any "and "much," isn't it? Do you agree with what Mr. McCloskey has stated?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Since this part, as far as I know, was provided to the Prosecutor in B/C/S, and what I have read was the B/C/S original. What the Prosecutor has is a translation which may not be correct. The exact translation is in the transcript. "Gvero cannot have any influence. He was a grammar school principal all his life."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. We can't help you or anyone else, for that matter, because we don't have the text in B/C/S, and even if we had it, we don't have -- we don't read it. We don't understand it. So we have to rely on the interpretation on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May I -- may I just explain, Your Honour? Because I discussed this with my learned friend Mr. Bourgon at the break because this is exactly the same difficulty as he had with PW-108. Of course, this interview was conducted by Mr. McCloskey in English, the witness answered in his own language, the answer was then translated immediately back to Mr. McCloskey. The English version which I have got is what Mr. McCloskey said and what Mr. McCloskey heard at the time from the interpreter. What Mr. Krgovic has, of course, is what the witness said at the time in B/C/S. In other words, it's been transcribed from the tape in the original B/C/S language. Therefore, what Mr. Krgovic in effect is saying is that the reliable answer is the one the witness gave at the time in B/C/S, the one that he's just read out, and that's precisely why he wanted it retranslated today. I hope that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you satisfied -- thank you, Mr. Josse. Are you satisfied with that explanation, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I agree with that. That's why I sat down, though I might disagree whether it's a reliable answer or not but I think the words that are used have been clarified and I trust Mr. Krgovic absolutely on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's proceed, Mr. Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you knew General Gvero and you said that during those days, you played chess with him often. That's what you said to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And your discussions and conversations with him focused mostly on chess; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'll now show you a document that is indicative of Gvero's job and preoccupations at the moment. Can we show 6D140, please? Sir, I don't think you had the opportunity to see this document at the time. It's a document whereby -- which the command of the Eastern Bosnia Corps sent to Gvero and it concerns documentation for the manufacturing of a giant plate. Do you know anything about it? Of a giant chess board, in fact.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, something similar to the giant chess board in the hotel in Kupari. It was a useful thing to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that hotel, you mean that hotel in Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Right. Han Pijesak is not a hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't need this document any more. Colonel, I'd like to ask you one thing. I asked you about the duties of General Gvero. In the Main Staff, were the assistants interchangeable? Did assistant commanders and chiefs of certain sectors, because Gvero was among other things chief for religious affairs, morale, et cetera, did Gvero ever perform the duties of General Tolimir or Djukic? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: I know that it's impossible to replace the logistical man or the man for morale because they don't go to the staff academy. They have special training. They go to a special school. I don't remember that anybody was ever assigned to replace the man for logistics or the man for morale. You can't put an engineer, mechanical engineer, to be Chief of Staff. So interchangeability never existed in the JNA and could not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And later, in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: We worked by the same laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Another question, a related one: The Prosecutor and Madam Fauveau showed you several combat reports that were passed on to the Supreme Command and that reached you in your sector. At that time, there were six corps in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And all these reports arrived from all corps on your desk?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout most of 1995, the focus of you operations personnel was on a particular theatre of war. Could you tell me which one and which corps was expected to face the greatest problems?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: The 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the one commanded by Talic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Not Talic. 2nd Krajina Corps. That's why Manojlo went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Kelecevic or Tomanic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: No. Talic was the commander of the 1st one and Tomanic replaced, I can't remember the name now. When Kupres was lost, Tomanic came to be the commander -- the new commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Why was that the focus of your attention at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Because territory was being lost, Kupres first, then the attack on Drvar so the whole territory of the Krajina Corps was in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And if I understand you well, that was the concern of General Gvero in view of his duties, the assistant for morale is most concerned not when the army is winning but when the army is losing?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA
utterances.text: Yes, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have about ten or 15 minutes left. I don't know if the Prosecution has any -- or maybe if there are any other colleagues, Mr. Sarapa, I don't know whether to speed up or to -- if there is going to be redirect and any cross from Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will not have any cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa, you're not having any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Nikolic? Sorry, Mr. Bourgon? My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If it can help in finishing with the witness today, we will have no questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Under 10 minutes. Will you have a re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Quite a bit. Then we have to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then, Your Honour, since I'm about to move to another topic that is completely different, maybe now is a good time to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. One moment. So we'll continue tomorrow afternoon, I think tomorrow, the sitting, isn't it? In the afternoon. Yes. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, if we do indeed continue tomorrow, then I would like to ask my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Your position is reserved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
